title: Quicksort
summary: Sorting by partitioning - the Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes, quicksort's average O(n log n) and worst-case O(n²), choosing pivots at random or by median of three, three-way partitioning for many duplicates, recursing on the smaller side, introsort (std::sort), and quickselect and std::nth_element for the k-th smallest element in linear time.

cards.q: When does quicksort with "last element as pivot" take O(n²)?
cards.a:
On input that is already sorted (or reversed)

Each partition then splits off just one element, so there are n levels of O(n) work.

Slowness on many equal elements

Equal elements are gathered in the middle and never touched again, so arrays full of duplicates no longer degrade quicksort.

cards.q: Why recurse on the smaller side and loop on the larger one?
cards.a:
It keeps the stack depth at O(log n)

Each recursive call handles at most half of the current range, so the stack cannot overflow (the time can still be O(n²)).

cards.q: What does std::nth_element(b, b + k, e) guarantee?
cards.a:
b + k holds the element sorting would put there

Everything before it is no larger and everything after no smaller, but neither side is sorted. It is quickselect: expected O(n).
